questions.prompt: A decision tree scores **1.00** on the training set and **0.89** on the test set. Which number tells you how it will do on new data?
choices: 1.00, because it learned from more data
0.89, the score on data it never saw
The average, 0.945
Neither; accuracy can't be measured
questions.explain: Only the held-out test score measures performance on unseen data. The perfect training score shows the tree memorised its examples (overfitting).

choices: Fitting a `StandardScaler` on the whole dataset, then splitting into train and test
Splitting first, then fitting the scaler on the training part only
Putting the scaler and model in one `Pipeline`
Using `stratify=y` in `train_test_split`
questions.explain: Fitting the scaler on all the data lets the test set's mean and spread influence training. Split first, or let a Pipeline do it for you.

questions.prompt: You try 20 values of `k` and keep the one with the best **test** score. What's wrong?
choices: Nothing; that's how tuning works
The test set has been used to choose the model, so its score is now optimistic
20 values is too few
KNN can't be tuned
questions.explain: Choosing by test score tunes the model to the test set, so it stops being a fair final exam. Choose with cross-validation on the training data, and use the test set once.

choices: It makes the split faster
It keeps each class's proportion the same in the train and test sets
It removes duplicate rows
It scales the features
questions.explain: Stratifying preserves the class balance in both parts, so an unlucky shuffle can't leave a class under-represented in the test set.

questions.prompt: Ten balanced classes. A `DummyClassifier` scores 0.10 and your model 0.12. What should you conclude?
choices: The model is 20% better, so it's good
The model has learned almost nothing beyond guessing
Accuracy is the wrong metric for ten classes
The test set is too big
questions.explain: The baseline shows guessing already gets 0.10. Beating it by 0.02 means the model barely uses the features; always judge a score against a baseline.
